title: Renoviction by-law and vacant home tax
subtitle: Also: city-owned land for affordable housing, source protection plan amendments, police board diversity plan and wastewater lab closure direction.
overview: The Committee of the Whole spent most of the afternoon on affordable housing. After hearing nine delegates, it recommended that staff begin developing a framework for a renoviction by-law and a rental replacement by-law in 2026, rather than waiting until 2027 as staff first proposed. This depends on $311,000 being included in the 2026 budget update {{vote:m8}}. Staff will also keep lobbying the province on tenancy law.

The committee also recommended that staff draft a complaint-based vacant home tax by-law at a four per cent rate, up from the two per cent staff proposed. This depends on $275,000 in the 2026 budget update. Councillors raised questions about exemptions, which will be worked out during by-law drafting. Staff agreed to report back by the end of the month on what it would take to speed up the work and on higher property standards fines for vacant homes.

The committee recommended that Council endorse an expanded city role in affordable housing, starting with fourplexes at 5 Normandy Drive and 7 Eastview Road {{vote:m9}}. It also approved a diversity plan for the Guelph Police Service Board {{vote:m2}} and recommended endorsing source protection plan amendments {{vote:m3}}. All of these recommendations go to Council for final decision. After a closed session, Council gave direction to staff on the wastewater lab closure.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff begin developing a framework for both by-laws in 2026, subject to $311,000 in the 2026 budget update, replacing staff's proposed report-back in 2027.
The committee recommended that staff draft a complaint-based vacant home tax by-law at a four per cent rate, subject to $275,000 in the 2026 budget update.
The committee recommended that staff keep advocating for Residential Tenancies Act changes on renovictions and report to Council on any impacts if the province changes the rules.
The committee recommended the combined, amended package on advocacy, the by-law framework and the vacant home tax {{vote:m8}}.

The committee recommended that Council endorse an expanded city role, with fourplexes at 5 Normandy Drive and 7 Eastview Road and a $3,406,150 budget funded by the Housing Accelerator Fund and $400,000 from the Affordable Housing reserve.
The committee recommended approving the Diversity Plan for the Guelph Police Service Board.
The committee recommended that Council endorse the draft water quantity policy amendments to the Grand River Source Protection Plan.

debate: Delegates from tenant and community groups, and a legal clinic representative, urged action in 2026 rather than 2027. They said renovation notices are rising, many tenants give up or take cash-for-keys deals, and a by-law would add oversight. They pointed to Hamilton, London and Toronto as models.

Staff said the data cannot show how many renovation notices lead to actual renovictions. They noted that most municipalities with a renoviction by-law also have a rental replacement by-law, and that provincial changes are uncertain. They said a by-law is a new service needing staff, legal and technology resources, so the timeline is about a year.

Several delegates asked for a four per cent vacant home tax with mandatory declarations, and for multi-unit buildings to be included. Staff said a complaint-based model costs less to run and that provincial rules limit the tax to residential-class properties. A councillor asked that exemptions, such as accessory units and estate settlements, be reviewed.
Delegates described long-vacant, deteriorating houses that neighbours see as safety and fire risks. This led to a request for a staff memo on higher property standards fines for vacant properties.

On the city-land fourplexes, councillors supported the new approach. They asked about parking at the sites, neighbourhood notification and whether an operator could serve deeper affordability. Staff said the units would be affordable by the provincial definition, and that the Housing Accelerator Fund timeline is tight.
